question.stem: A deep-space probe is powered by a radioisotope source containing plutonium-238. Plutonium-238 decays by alpha emission with a half-life of 88 years. The thermal energy released in the source is partly converted to electrical energy; the rest is radiated into space.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.question: Plutonium-238 ($^{238}_{94}\text{Pu}$) decays to an isotope of uranium (U). Write down the equation for this decay.
markscheme: nucleon number 234 and proton number 92 for uranium ✓

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.question: At launch the activity of the source is $2.7 \times 10^{15}$ Bq and each decay releases 5.6 MeV. Show that the thermal power produced by the source at launch is about 2.4 kW.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.question: Determine the thermal power produced by the source 264 years after launch.
markscheme: $\dfrac{264}{88} = 3$ half-lives, so the power falls by a factor of $2^{3} = 8$ ✓
Allow ECF from (a)(ii); accept 293 to 312 W

mistakes.feedback: Three half-lives halve the power three times: divide by 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, not by 6.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.question: Outline why an alpha emitter is a good choice for this power source.
markscheme: alpha particles are strongly ionising / have a very short range, so they are absorbed within the source itself ✓
so (almost) all their energy becomes thermal energy in the source, and little shielding is needed to protect the instruments ✓

parts.label: b(i)
parts.question: Before launch, the source sits inside an aluminium casing of mass 12 kg. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$. If its cooling system failed, how quickly would the temperature of the casing start to rise? Calculate this rate. Assume all the thermal power goes into the casing.
markscheme: Allow ECF from (a)(ii); accept 0.215 to 0.233 $\text{K s}^{-1}$

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.question: In space, the radiator fins have a total surface area of 1.2 $\text{m}^{2}$ and radiate 2.3 kW. Determine the temperature of the fins. Assume they behave as a black body.

mistakes.feedback: The power radiated depends on T⁴: take the fourth root, not the square root.

parts.label: c(i)
parts.question: The electrical power output is 110 W at a potential difference of 28 V. Calculate the output current.

parts.label: c(ii)
parts.question: Calculate, as a percentage, the efficiency of the conversion of thermal power to electrical power at launch.

parts.label: c(iii)
parts.question: The cables connecting the source to the instruments have a total resistance of 0.15 Ω. Calculate the power dissipated in the cables.

parts.label: d(i)
parts.question: The probe later orbits Saturn in a circular orbit of radius $1.2 \times 10^{9}$ m. The mass of Saturn is $5.68 \times 10^{26}$ kg. Calculate the gravitational field strength due to Saturn at the probe.

parts.label: d(ii)
parts.question: Explain why a loose object inside the orbiting probe floats, even though there is a gravitational field at the probe.
markscheme: the probe and the object are both in free fall, accelerating towards Saturn with the same acceleration $g$ ✓
so there is no contact (normal) force between them: the object does not press on the probe, and floats relative to it ✓

A0.what: activity of the source at launch

Prad.what: power radiated by the fins in space

Af.what: surface area of the radiator fins

rs.what: radius of the probe's orbit around Saturn

parts.label: a(i)
parts.examinerNote: An alpha particle carries away 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Both sides must balance.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.examinerNote: Power = decays per second × energy per decay, with 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.examinerNote: Whole numbers of half-lives only (SL). The power is proportional to the activity.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.examinerNote: Short range means the energy stays in the source as heat, and the radiation does not escape to damage electronics.

parts.label: b(i)
parts.examinerNote: Q = mcΔT per second. Using 2.4 kW gives a value about 1 % lower, inside the range.

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.examinerNote: Stefan–Boltzmann law for a black body; in a vacuum, radiation is the only way the fins lose energy.

parts.label: c(i)
parts.examinerNote: Electrical power P = IV, rearranged for the current.

parts.label: c(ii)
parts.examinerNote: Useful power out over total power in. 110/2400 gives 4.6 %, also accepted.

parts.label: c(iii)
parts.examinerNote: The cables carry the full output current.

parts.label: d(i)
parts.examinerNote: Saturn treated as a point mass at its centre.

parts.label: d(ii)
parts.examinerNote: Gravity provides the centripetal acceleration of both; "weightlessness" is the absence of a supporting force, not the absence of gravity.
